turns.content: My wedding is six weeks away. My closest friend Rohan is supposed to be in my haldi and give a toast — he's been my guy since first year of college. But every time I bring up his travel from Bangalore he just says "let's see, I'll definitely try." Should I just book his flight myself and be done with it?

Hey, first of all, take a breath. Six weeks is soon, but you definitely have time to sort this out without losing your mind. I completely get why you're considering just booking it yourself—it's stressful when the person who's supposed to be a cornerstone of your day keeps handing you that fuzzy "I'll try."

Before you go ahead and book it, I'd gently give him a real, low-pressure chat (voice or in person, texts always flatten tone). You could say something like: *"Hey, I'm getting a little stressed about wedding logistics and I really need you in the haldi and for my toast. Are you actually able to make it to Bangalore? If work, money, or anything else is making it tough, just tell me straight. I'd rather figure out a backup now than leave it hanging."*

Sometimes friends stall because they're overwhelmed, juggling something they haven't mentioned, or just hate saying no to people they care about. Giving him a clear, guilt-free off-ramp often gets you the honest answer you actually need. If he says yes, wonderful. If he's still noncommittal or says no, then you can decide whether booking it as a surprise gift makes sense for your friendship and your peace of mind.

You're allowed to want what you need on your day, and a friend who's truly been in your corner will respect you asking clearly. However it plays out, you'll have closure instead of this hanging anxiety. You've got this. 💛

I checked, flights are like nine thousand return. Not crazy. He switched jobs a couple of months back, some startup. And lately his replies are two words where he used to send voice notes. I'm telling myself he's busy but it's been weeks of this.

Hey, I hear you. That shift in how he's communicating—going from those long voice notes to two-word replies—is really noticeable, and it's completely valid to feel unsettled by it. Startups can be all-consuming, sure, but it's also fair to name that it's been weeks of this and that you miss the old rhythm.

I get why you're thinking about just booking the flight. It's not even that expensive, and honestly, part of you probably just wants to remove the friction so he shows up. But before you do, I'd gently untangle two things: the wedding logistics, and this quiet distance that's been creeping in.

You could send him a quick voice note (since that's how you two usually connect) and say something like: *"Hey, I've noticed things have been pretty quiet lately and I miss our chats. I also need to know clearly if you can make it to Bangalore for the haldi. If yes, I'll gladly book the flight for you since I know the new job is heavy. If you can't, I totally get it—just tell me straight so I can plan accordingly."*

That removes the "I'll try" limbo and gives him a clear, kind way to either step up or step back. If he's just drowning in work, the offer might actually be a relief. If he's drifting, you'll finally get the honest answer you deserve. Either way, you stop carrying this quiet anxiety alone.

You've been each other's person for years. A real friend will honor that, even when life gets messy. However it plays out, you're not being selfish for needing clarity. I'm right here with you. 💛

Honestly it's starting to hurt now. If he actually cared he would have just said yes on day one, no? I'm thinking I should just call him tonight and ask him straight — "bro, are you coming or not, yes or no." At least I'll know where I stand.

Hey, it's completely okay that this is hurting. When someone who's been your constant suddenly goes quiet and leaves you hanging, it's natural to feel like maybe you don't matter as much as you thought. But before that thought takes root, give yourself a little grace—and give him a little bit too. Most of the time, people don't avoid saying "I can't" because they don't care. They're just overwhelmed, terrified of disappointing you, or bad at setting boundaries when life gets loud. New jobs, mental load, even guilt can make someone freeze and say "I'll try" instead of "no."

Calling him tonight to ask straight is actually the healthiest move you can make. Clarity beats waiting in limbo, especially with a wedding this close. When you call, you don't need to over-explain or soften it into a question. Just say something like: *"Bro, I need a straight yes or no. I'm finalizing the haldi plans and I really want you there, but I can't keep planning around 'maybe.' Just tell me where you're at."*

If he says yes, you can offer to book the flight right then. If he says no, or gives you another fuzzy answer, let that be the answer. It'll sting, but it'll also lift this quiet dread off your shoulders. And honestly? A friendship that's been solid for years can survive a hard conversation. You're not being dramatic—you're being responsible to yourself and to the day you're building.

However it goes, you're not carrying it alone. I'm right here with you. 💛

My fiancée says I'm overthinking and he's probably just swamped. But this is the same guy who took an overnight bus to be at my sister's wedding in 2019. Something has changed and I can't figure out what, and I hate that I'm angry at him two weeks before my haldi.

Hey, it makes so much sense that you're feeling this way. That 2019 bus trip vs. the two-word replies now is a real contrast, and your brain is just trying to make sense of it. You're not overthinking—you're paying attention. And it's totally okay that you're angry, especially with everything else swirling around the haldi. You're not a bad friend for needing consistency from someone who's been your constant for years.

I get why your fiancée is trying to give him the benefit of the doubt and protect your peace. New jobs can be genuinely all-consuming, and she's probably coming from a place of love. But her perspective doesn't erase your feelings. You're allowed to miss the old rhythm and feel unsettled by the shift, even if you can't pinpoint exactly why it's happening yet.

When you call him tonight, try to keep it grounded in what you need, not in what you're assuming he's doing wrong. Something like: *"Bro, I need a straight yes or no on Bangalore. I'm not trying to guilt you—I just need clarity for the haldi plans. If you're swamped or something else is going on, just say it. I'd rather know now than keep guessing."* That strips away the limbo and gives him a clear, low-pressure way to be honest.

Whatever he says, please don't carry guilt for feeling hurt. Friendships naturally shift when life gets heavy, but that doesn't mean your bond is broken. You can still care about him and also protect your own peace on your day. However it plays out, you're not alone in this. I'm right here with you. 💛
